0.title: When Their Joy Stings
0.essay:
A friend tells you her good news. You smile, you say all the right things, and you mean some of them. But somewhere underneath, something sinks. Later you find yourself picking at her success, or scrolling past it, or quietly replaying it. If you know that small, sour ache, this study is for you.

An old ache with a name

The Bible calls it envy. It is one of the oldest sins in the world and one of the least confessed. People will admit to anger, worry or even lust long before they will admit, “I could not bear that they had it and I did not.” Envy hides well. It dresses up as fairness, realism or a sharp eye for other people’s faults.

Yet Scripture does not treat envy as a small thing. “A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot” (Proverbs 14:30). It eats the person who carries it, and it spoils friendships, families and churches.

You are not unusual if you feel it. And God does not leave envious people in their envy. He is far more generous than our hearts imagine.

Where we are going

We will name the sting in ordinary words, and tell envy apart from jealousy. We will look at some of the Bible’s honest portraits of envy, and ask what envy reveals about our hearts. Then we will hear the gospel’s answer: a generous Father, a gift-giving Saviour and a body in which every member is needed. We will end with practical wisdom for the moment the sting comes, and for the days afterwards.

The study Contentment & Anxiety has a chapter on the enemies of contentment, including comparison, and this study builds on it rather than repeating it. The study The Fear of Man deals with the longing for approval, which is a close cousin of envy.

The chapters

The Sting; Envy’s Long Shadow; What Envy Reveals; A Generous Father; Many Members, One Joy; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

When did you last feel a sting at someone else’s good news? What did they have that you wanted, and what did you tell yourself about them afterwards?

1.title: The Sting
1.essay:
It often comes as a small jolt. A colleague is promoted. A friend’s child wins a place you hoped your child would win. Someone at church is asked to lead, and you were not. Your face stays pleasant, but inside something tightens: why them, and not me?

Where it bites

Envy is rarely general. It tends to bite in the places that matter most to us.

Success. A friend’s business takes off. A younger colleague overtakes you. A neighbour moves to the bigger house. Gifts. Someone sings, speaks, writes or leads with an ease you have never had, and everyone notices. Family. A brother is the favourite. A sister’s marriage looks happier than yours. Friends announce a pregnancy while you are still waiting and praying. Other people’s children seem to be doing so well. Looks. Someone is slimmer, younger-looking, better dressed, more noticed. Ministry. Another church grows while yours struggles. Another speaker is invited back. Another small group leader seems to have all the fruit. Social media. Every day the phone brings a stream of other people’s best moments: holidays, weddings, new jobs, perfect kitchens. We see their highlights and measure our ordinary days against them.

Notice that envy usually targets people near us. We rarely envy a film star. We envy the person one rung above us, in our own field, our own family, our own church. The closer the person, the sharper the sting.

How envy hides

Envy is a sin that hates to be seen. It rarely says, “I want what she has.” It says, “She’s been very lucky,” or “He knows the right people,” or “I don’t see what all the fuss is about.” It looks for flaws in the person we envy, and is secretly pleased to find them. It may even feel a small, shameful pleasure when they stumble. That is envy’s other face: sorrow at another’s good, and gladness at another’s harm.

Scripture is not shy about naming it. Paul lists envy among “the works of the flesh” alongside “enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries” (Galatians 5:20–21). He describes life before grace as “passing our days in malice and envy” (Titus 3:3). Peter tells believers to “put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander” (1 Peter 2:1). Envy keeps bad company.

Envy and jealousy

In everyday English the two words are often used for the same thing, and the Bible’s own words overlap too. But it helps to tell them apart.

Envy looks at what someone else has and resents it. It says, “I want what you have,” and often, “I wish you did not have it.” It involves two people: me and the one I envy.

Jealousy, in its proper sense, guards what is rightly mine. It says, “I will not lose what belongs to me.” It involves three: me, the one I love, and a rival. That kind of jealousy can be good. God calls himself “a jealous God” (Exodus 20:5), because his people belong to him and he will not share them with idols. Paul could say, “I feel a divine jealousy for you” (2 Corinthians 11:2), because he longed for the church to stay faithful to Christ. A husband or wife rightly feels a protective jealousy for their marriage.

But jealousy goes wrong when it becomes possessive, suspicious or controlling, or when we are “jealous” over something that was never ours to keep, such as a friend’s attention or our place as the most admired person in the room. Then it slides into envy. Much of what we call jealousy is really envy. When Genesis says that Joseph’s brothers “were jealous of him” (Genesis 37:11), it is describing exactly this: resentment at the favour shown to another.

An example

A woman in her forties sings in the church choir. When a newcomer with a beautiful voice is given the solo at Christmas, she tells her husband the girl is “a bit showy”. She notices herself hoping the performance will not go well, and is ashamed. On the night, the solo is lovely. She claps with everyone else, then drives home in silence, feeling small and strangely tired.

Why it matters

“A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot” (Proverbs 14:30). Envy steals joy from the envier long before it harms anyone else. It turns friends into rivals, and good news into bad news. And “love does not envy or boast” (1 Corinthians 13:4), so envy is a quiet failure of love.

But to name it is not to be crushed by it. The God who shows us our envy is the God who forgives envious people, and who has given his Son for them. Seeing it is the first step towards freedom.

For reflection

In which area does envy most often bite you: success, gifts, family, looks, ministry or social media? Whom do you tend to envy, and how close are they to you? How does your envy usually disguise itself? Can you think of a time when you felt a quiet pleasure at someone else’s setback?

2.title: Envy’s Long Shadow
2.essay:
The Bible tells the story of envy with painful honesty. From the first family onward, it shows envy starting small, in a fallen face or a sideways look, and growing into something that can wreck lives. These portraits are not there to make us feel superior. They are mirrors.

Cain: a fallen face

Cain and Abel both brought offerings. “And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering, but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell” (Genesis 4:4–5). The trouble was not Abel. Abel had done Cain no harm. The trouble was that God’s favour rested on his brother.

God came to Cain with a warning and an invitation: “If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it” (Genesis 4:7). Envy is pictured as a wild animal waiting at the door. Cain did not master it, and the first murder followed. John later explains why Cain killed his brother: “Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous” (1 John 3:12). Envy often hates in others the goodness it lacks.

Saul: an eye that would not let go

After David killed Goliath, the women of Israel came out singing, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7). It was a song of victory for Israel. Saul heard only the numbers. “And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him” (1 Samuel 18:8). Then comes one of the saddest lines in the Old Testament: “And Saul eyed David from that day on” (1 Samuel 18:9).

Saul was the king. He had everything. Yet one song about someone else ruined it all. Within a day he was hurling a spear. In time “Saul was David’s enemy continually” (1 Samuel 18:29). Envy kept him awake, drove away his peace, and in the end cost him his throne and his son’s friendship.

Set beside Saul his son Jonathan, who had more reason than anyone to envy David. Jonathan was the heir. Yet he loved David, gave him his own robe and sword, and later said, “You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you” (1 Samuel 23:17). Same family, same rival, two very different hearts.

Joseph’s brothers: a family wound

Jacob “loved Joseph more than any other of his sons” (Genesis 37:3) and gave him a special robe. “But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him” (Genesis 37:3–4). Their father’s favouritism was wrong, and it wounded them. But envy turned a wound into a plot. “Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits … and we will see what will become of his dreams” (Genesis 37:20).

Stephen summed it up centuries later: “the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him” (Acts 7:9). Those last words matter. God was at work even through their envy, and years later Joseph could say, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Family envy is often rooted in real hurt. God sees the hurt, and he can bring good even out of what envy has done.

Asaph: an honest believer

Not every envier in Scripture is a villain. Asaph was a temple musician and a man of faith. Yet he confessed, “For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (Psalm 73:3). He looked at people who ignored God and seemed to do very well, and he began to wonder whether faithfulness was worth it: “All in vain have I kept my heart clean” (Psalm 73:13).

Two things in Asaph’s story are a model for us. First, he kept quiet before others while he wrestled: “If I had said, ‘I will speak thus,’ I would have betrayed the generation of your children” (Psalm 73:15). He did not spread his bitterness. Second, he was brutally honest with God afterwards: “When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you” (Psalm 73:21–22). Envy had made him less than human. The study Contentment & Anxiety traces how God turned Asaph’s heart in the sanctuary, until he could say that God was his portion forever.

The pattern

Look at the steps. A face falls. An eye fixes on another person. Words turn sour. Then hands act. James traces the same path: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice” (James 3:16). Very few of us will throw a spear. But the same seed can grow into gossip, coldness, sabotage or a friendship quietly dropped.

An example

Two brothers run the family business their father built. When the father praises the younger brother at a retirement dinner, the elder says nothing, but over the next year he begins to undermine him in small ways: a missed email, a decision questioned in front of staff. It takes a long talk with his pastor before he sees that the old childhood ache, “Dad always liked him better”, has been steering him for decades.

For reflection

Which of these portraits is closest to your own experience: Cain’s fallen face, Saul’s watching eye, the brothers’ family wound, or Asaph’s quiet doubt? What does Jonathan show you about the alternative? Is there a real hurt beneath your envy that you need to bring to God? What has your envy already done, in words or actions?

3.title: What Envy Reveals
3.essay:
Envy is not only a feeling to be resisted. It is a signal. It tells us something about what our hearts are leaning on and what we believe about God. If we listen to it honestly, envy can show us exactly where we need the gospel.

A good thing made ultimate

Haman was the second most powerful man in the Persian empire. One evening he gathered his friends and listed his blessings: his riches, his sons, his promotions, and a private invitation to dine with the queen. Then he said, “Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate” (Esther 5:13).

All this is worth nothing. That is the voice of envy. It can make a person with almost everything miserable over the one thing someone else has, in Haman’s case the honour of a man who would not bow to him. When a good thing such as success, a gift, a family, a body or a ministry becomes the thing we must have to feel all right, it has become what the Bible calls an idol: a good thing made ultimate. And idols are never satisfied while someone else has more of them.

So when you feel the sting, ask: what does this person have that I think I need in order to be happy, secure or significant? The answer usually points straight to the idol.

A scarcity view of God’s goodness

Jesus told a parable about a landowner who hired workers for his vineyard at different hours of the day. Some worked from early morning, others from the third, sixth and ninth hours, and a few only for the last hour. At evening he paid them all a full day’s wage. The first workers “grumbled at the master of the house, saying, ‘These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat’” (Matthew 20:11–12).

The master answered, “Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? … Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?” (Matthew 20:13–15). The Greek of that last question speaks literally of an evil eye: is your eye evil because I am good? Among Jews of the time an “evil eye” meant a grudging, stingy spirit.

Notice what happened. The early workers were not cheated. They received exactly what was promised. Their complaint was not that the master was unfair to them, but that he was generous to someone else. Envy quietly assumes that God’s goodness is like a cake: if someone else gets a big slice, there is less for me. It treats God as a stingy master, and other people’s blessings as a loss to us.

The elder brother in Luke 15 shows the same heart. When his younger brother came home and the father threw a feast, “he was angry and refused to go in” (Luke 15:28). His complaint gives him away: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (Luke 15:29). He had lived in his father’s house as a servant counting his wages, not as a son enjoying his father. So his brother’s welcome felt like robbery.

Comparison as a ladder of worth

Underneath much envy lies a ladder. We place ourselves and everyone else on rungs, by looks, income, gifts, children, followers or fruitfulness, and we feel our worth by how high we stand. Someone else rising feels like us falling. C. S. Lewis put it sharply in Mere Christianity: “Pride gets no pleasure out of having something, only out of having more of it than the next man.” Envy is pride’s wounded twin. Pride enjoys being above; envy suffers from being below. Both are standing on the same ladder.

Paul offers a different way to look at our work: “But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor” (Galatians 6:4). Our task is faithfulness with what God has given us, not a higher rung than our neighbour. And he asks a question that saws through the ladder: “What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). If everything is gift, then there is nothing left to compete over.

An example

A young pastor notices that whenever a nearby church announces a new building or a full baptism service, he feels flat for days. One morning he writes down honestly what he fears: that a small church means he is a small pastor. He sees that he has been measuring his worth by attendance. He prays, “Lord, these are your people, not my scoreboard.” The next week he sends the other pastor a note of thanks for the gospel work being done in their town.

Mercy in the mirror

Seeing these things in ourselves is humbling. But God shows us our envy not to shame us, but to call us home. The father went out to the angry elder son too, and “entreated him” (Luke 15:28). God does the same for us.

For reflection

When you envy someone, what do you think they have that you need? Do you ever treat God’s goodness as if it were in short supply? Where do you place yourself on the ladder of comparison, and who is just above you? Read 1 Corinthians 4:7 slowly. Which of your gifts do you most easily forget that you received?

4.title: A Generous Father
4.essay:
The cure for envy is not to want less, nor simply to try harder to be pleased for others. It is to see how generous God has been to us in Christ. When the Father’s generosity fills our view, other people’s blessings stop looking like threats.

All that is mine is yours

Return to the elder brother standing outside the feast. His father does not scold him. He comes out, pleads with him, and says, “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). The elder brother had been envying a goat while the whole estate was his. He had been counting wages while living in his father’s love.

That is the gospel’s first answer to envy. In Christ, God has not given us a small portion while others get the large ones. He has given us himself. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3). Every spiritual blessing. Not the leftovers.

Paul even turns the Corinthians’ rivalry over teachers upside down: “So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future, all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). The gifted preacher you envy is not your rival. He is God’s gift to you.

Identity given, not earned

Envy grows on the ladder of comparison because we are trying to earn a worth we do not believe we already have. The gospel gives us a worth that is not on the ladder at all. When the disciples came back from their mission thrilled by their success, Jesus redirected their joy: “Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

Your deepest identity is not your job title, your looks, your family’s achievements or your ministry’s size. It is that you belong to Christ, your name written in heaven, adopted by the Father, joined to the Son by the Spirit. No one else’s promotion can touch that. No one’s photographs can make it smaller.

We are all eleventh-hour workers

The parable of the labourers ends, “So the last will be first, and the first last” (Matthew 20:16). Once we see ourselves rightly, we discover that we are not the early-morning workers at all. We are the ones hired at the eleventh hour, who did almost nothing and were paid in full. Salvation is all grace. “But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

A person who knows they have received a whole day’s wage for an hour’s work cannot easily begrudge others the same kindness. Grace received makes grace for others a joy rather than an injury.

The one who did not grasp

Envy grasps. It reaches for what another has. Christ did the opposite. Though he was in the form of God, he “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). He who owned everything let go of it for us.

And envy put him on the cross. Pilate “perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up” (Mark 15:10). The religious leaders could not bear the crowds following Jesus, so they handed him over to die. Think of it: the Saviour was killed by the very sin he came to forgive. He bore our envy in his body, and he prayed for those who crucified him. There is no envy in us so dark that his blood cannot cleanse it.

Then Paul draws the great conclusion: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). If God has given his Son, he will not withhold anything we truly need. He is not a stingy master. He is a Father who gave the best gift first.

God’s good gifts, God’s good timing

This does not mean we will receive everything we want, or what others have. God gives different gifts, at different times, to different people, for his own wise purposes. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). The gift your friend has received came from your Father too. To begrudge it is to quarrel with him; to give thanks for it is to share his joy. Where you are waiting for something good and others have received it first, the study Disappointment & Waiting may help.

The psalmist, looking at his own lot, could say, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance” (Psalm 16:5–6). That is the voice of someone who has stopped looking over the fence.

An example

A single man in his thirties dreads weddings. He has stopped going to some. One evening his small group reads Luke 15, and the words “all that is mine is yours” lodge in him. He still longs to marry, and tells God so. But he begins to pray, before each wedding, “Father, you have not forgotten me. Help me to enjoy your kindness to them.” At the next one, to his surprise, he dances.

For reflection

Have you been living as a son or daughter in the Father’s house, or as a servant counting wages? What does Ephesians 1:3 say you already have in Christ? How does it change your view of others’ blessings to see yourself as an eleventh-hour worker? Read Romans 8:32 and ask: what am I afraid God will withhold from me?

5.title: Many Members, One Joy
5.essay:
God does not only free us from envy. He gives us something better to do with other people’s gifts and successes: to share in them. In the body of Christ, another member’s honour is not my loss. It is part of my joy.

The foot and the hand

Paul pictured the church as a body. “If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,’ that would not make it any less a part of the body” (1 Corinthians 12:15). The foot is comparing itself with the hand, and concluding that it does not count. That is envy’s voice inside the church: I am not the preacher, the singer, the leader, so I do not matter.

Paul answers: “But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose” (1 Corinthians 12:18). Your place is not an accident or a second prize. God chose it. And he adds that “the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (1 Corinthians 12:22). The quiet servant, the faithful pray-er, the one who sets out chairs and visits the lonely: these are not lesser members. The body cannot do without them.

Gifts differ by God’s design. “Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them” (Romans 12:6), whether serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading or showing mercy. Peter says the same: “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace” (1 Peter 4:10). Varied grace. God loves variety. He did not make a church of eyes.

Rejoicing together

Then comes the verse that turns envy inside out: “If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together” (1 Corinthians 12:26). When my hand is healed, my foot does not sulk. In a body, one part’s good is every part’s good.

So Paul commands, “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Many people find the second half easier. It is often easier to weep with the struggling than to rejoice with the flourishing, because their sorrow does not threaten us. Rejoicing with others is one of the clearest signs that grace is at work in us. “Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12:10). Imagine a church where people compete to celebrate one another.

John the Baptist: the friend of the bridegroom

John the Baptist had crowds, disciples and fame. Then Jesus began his ministry, and the crowds moved. John’s disciples were worried: “look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him” (John 3:26). It was the perfect moment for envy.

John’s answer begins with gift: “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven” (John 3:27). His ministry had been given; it could be taken back, and that was God’s right. Then he describes himself as the best man at a wedding: “The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete. He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:29–30).

John did not grit his teeth as his crowds shrank. His joy was complete. He was not the bridegroom, and he did not want to be. His joy was in Christ’s joy. The study Humility & Pride looks at John’s humility; here notice his gladness. The best man does not envy the groom. He has the best seat at the wedding.

Others who chose joy

When two men began prophesying in the camp without Moses’ permission, young Joshua urged him to stop them. Moses answered, “Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29). He was glad for God to use others.

In prison Paul learned that some were preaching Christ “from envy and rivalry” (Philippians 1:15), hoping to hurt him. His reply is astonishing: “What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice” (Philippians 1:18). He cared more about Christ’s name than his own.

And when the risen Jesus told Peter how he would die, Peter immediately looked at John and asked, “Lord, what about this man?” Jesus replied, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!” (John 21:21–22). That is the word Jesus speaks to every comparing heart. What is that to you? You follow me.

Contentment and its fruit

Rejoicing with others grows best in the soil of contentment: learning to receive our own portion from God with thanks. The study Contentment & Anxiety explores that soil in depth. Here we only add that contentment is not merely a private peace. It turns outward. A content heart has room to celebrate.

An example

Two women started a toddler group at their church together. One is outgoing and the parents adore her; the other does the planning and washing up. For a while the second woman feels invisible. Then she reads 1 Corinthians 12 and realises the group would collapse without her lists. She begins thanking God for her friend’s warmth, and tells her friend so. Their friendship deepens, and the group grows.

For reflection

Where in your church or family do you feel like the foot envying the hand? What gift has God given you to use for others, however hidden? Whose good news could you rejoice in this week, in words or actions? Hear Jesus say to you, “What is that to you? You follow me!” What would it mean to take that seriously?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
Envy usually strikes without warning: a message, a photograph, an announcement at church. The gospel truths of this study are meant for exactly that moment, and for the days afterwards when the sting lingers. Here is some practical wisdom, offered not as a way to earn God’s favour, but as ways to live from the favour Christ has already won.

In the moment: name it

When the sting comes, call it what it is, at least to yourself and to God. “Lord, I feel envy. I wish I had what they have.” That simple honesty takes away envy’s disguise. It is no longer “a fair point about their luck”. It is a sin, and sin can be confessed and forgiven. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

Then remember who you are. You might pray one of the verses from this study: “all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31), or “What is that to you? You follow me!” (John 21:22). You are not losing anything when someone else is blessed.

Guard your words

Asaph kept his bitterness from his community while he wrestled. Do the same. Envy loves to leak out in a small barb, a faint-praise remark, or a “Have you heard about…?” that is really gossip. Before you speak about the person you envy, ask whether your words will build them up. If not, say nothing for now.

Pray for the one you envy

This may be the most powerful practice of all. Pray for the person by name, and ask God to bless them in the very area where you envy them. “Lord, prosper her business.” “Bless his ministry.” “Give them joy in their new baby.” At first it may feel like praying through gritted teeth. Pray anyway. It is very hard to keep resenting someone you are regularly asking God to bless. Jesus told us to pray even for enemies (Matthew 5:44). How much more for a friend whose only offence is being blessed.

Give thanks, specifically

Envy looks over the fence; gratitude looks at what is in your own hands. “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). Some people find it helps to write down three particular gifts from God each day, especially in the area where envy bites. If you envy someone’s family, give thanks for your own people by name. If you envy someone’s gifts, give thanks for the gifts God has given you and ask how to use them.

Celebrate others out loud

Rejoicing with those who rejoice is not only a feeling to wait for. It is something to do. Send the message of congratulations. Go to the celebration. Tell a friend, “I loved your talk,” or “Your garden is beautiful.” Thank God publicly for someone else’s fruit. Often the feelings follow the actions. And let admiration teach you: if someone has a gift or grace you lack, learn from them. Scripture tells us to consider the faith of good leaders and “imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7). Envy wants to tear down; admiration wants to learn.

Wise habits with social media

Social media did not invent envy, but it feeds it many times a day. Notice which accounts or apps leave you feeling discontent, and mute, unfollow or delete them for a season. Set limits on when and how long you scroll. Remember that you are seeing highlights, chosen and often edited, not whole lives. And try using it to rejoice: when you see someone’s good news, pray a sentence of thanks for them before you scroll on.

When it goes deeper

Sometimes envy is tangled with deeper pain. Endless comparison about looks can feed self-loathing or an eating disorder. Envy of others’ lives can sit alongside low mood or depression. If that is you, please see a doctor or a qualified counsellor. That is not a failure of faith; God often gives help through such means, and medicine, where it is prescribed, is a good gift. The study Depression & the Christian may also help.

If comparison ever leads to thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. You are precious to God.

And if envy has already done damage, a friendship cooled or a colleague undermined, it may be right to put things right. The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation can help with that.

Do not fight alone

Tell a trusted Christian friend which kind of envy troubles you most, and ask them to pray and to ask you how it is going. Envy grows in secret and shrinks in the light.

An example

A mother of three young children finds that a school friend’s posts about travel and career leave her flat every evening. She mutes the account for a month, and each night writes down three things she is thankful for. She also begins praying for her friend by name. When the month is over she unmutes her, sees a photo of her friend’s new promotion, and finds she can honestly type, “So happy for you!” She still has hard days. But the posts no longer set the tone of her evenings.

Further reading

Melissa B. Kruger’s The Envy of Eve is a warm, practical book on covetousness and contentment.

Growth here is slow, and envy will return. That is not defeat. Each time you turn from comparing to giving thanks, from grasping to praying, you are learning to live as what you already are: a beloved child in a generous Father’s house, where all that is his is yours.

For reflection

Which of these practices would help you most when the sting comes, and which in the days afterwards? Whom will you pray for by name this week, asking God to bless them? What change to your use of social media would help your heart? Is there someone you need to celebrate, or something envy has damaged that you need to put right?
